conbody.p: As previously mentioned, the current trend for statutory damages in copyright litigation is often arbitrary, inconsistent, and excessive. The impressive ratio of damages to theft in Capitol v. Thomas (~35,000 to 1), is a testament to the corporate greed that the current system of copyright litigation enables. While the CASE Act attempts to amend this, capping damages at $30,000, this is still a large price tag for the average American. But, holders deserve an effective way to protect their expressive works; copyright violation is a civil wrong deserving of a remedy. The cost to download a typical music file on iTunes is around $1.29. Using this metric, were someone to illegally download around 20 music files, the total in theft rounds out to around $26.00. In Hashimoto & Samuelson’s write up of a workshop created to discuss the implementation of the CASE Act, they point out that given precedent, claimants are likely to demand statutory damages in the maximum amount no matter the case. In the case of the $26.00 thief, with an award of $30,000 to the claimant, this is still a ratio of ~1100 to 1. Were damages to be capped at around $5,000, lowering the $26.00 thief’s damage payment ratio to ~192 to 1, this would deter those who seek only to use copyright litigation as an independent revenue stream while keeping defendants from dealing with fines and fees that have the potential to ruin their lives. While this ratio is still rather unbalanced, it’s a start, aligning more closely with the U.S. Supreme Court’s guidance: few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio between punitive and compensatory damages, to a significant degree, will satisfy due process.

One thing to note about lowering the cap on statutory damages is the cost-benefit ratio. If the recovery of damages for a claimant is expected to be only around $1,000, attorney fees might heavily outweigh such a modest award. While this lowers the potential for holders to litigate violations of their copyright solely based on financial motivations, it also lowers the amount of attorneys who would be willing to take on such cases. Amending §412 so that holders are eligible for statutory damages and attorney fees could amend this issue, so might increasing the availability of pro bono or low-cost representation. The issue of return on investment needs to be addressed while attempting to eliminate copyright abuse.
